t: Lexicographically Smallest Negated Permutation Summing to Target
o: The absolute values must be 1..n, each optionally negated. Base sum S = n(n+1)/2; negating a value v lowers the sum by 2v, so we need a subset N with sum(N) = (S − target)/2, requiring |target| ≤ S and matching parity. Lexicographic smallness favors negating large values at the front: greedily scan v = n down to 1 and negate v whenever the remaining deficit is ≥ v (every remainder up to v(v−1)/2 is then reachable by smaller values). Output the negated values in decreasing order followed by the rest in increasing order — e.g. n=3, target=0 → [-3,1,2].
k: Solvable iff |target| ≤ S and (S − target) is even; the deficit halves to a subset-sum target.
Greedy largest-first subset selection always hits the exact deficit, and placing negated (large-first) values before positives yields the lexicographically smallest array.

a.i: Compute the required reduction R = S − target. Scan values from n down to 1, negating each value that fits in the remaining halved deficit; emit negatives descending then positives ascending.
s: If |target| > S or (S − target) is odd, return [].
rem = (S − target) / 2; for v = n..1, if rem ≥ v negate v and subtract.
Answer = negated list (descending) + remaining values ascending.
a.t: O(n) — one greedy scan plus one output pass
a.sp: O(n) for the flag array and output

w: The correctness hinges on two facts: greedy largest-first always realizes any deficit ≤ S (after choosing v, the residual is < v and representable by 1..v−1), and front-loading large negatives is lexicographically optimal. Pitfalls: 64-bit sums (target up to 1e10), and missing the parity impossibility check. Follow-up: lexicographically largest arrangement, or count how many arrangements achieve the target.
